title: Introduction to forrest
text:
forrest() draws a forest plot from any data frame with one row per estimate and columns for the point estimate and the confidence limits. The rows can be regression coefficients, subgroup estimates, studies in a meta-analysis or exposure categories. The package’s only dependency is tinyplot, and it accepts data frames, tibbles and data.tables.
This vignette shows each feature on a small example. The data in every example are invented for illustration.

title: Introduction to forrest
text:
Basic forest plot
A call needs three column names: estimate, lower and upper. Here they hold coefficients from a linear model of systolic blood pressure (SBP).

dat <- data.frame(
  predictor = c("Age (per 10 y)", "Female sex", "BMI (per 5 kg/m²)",
                "Current smoker", "Physically active"),
  estimate  = c( 0.18, -0.42,  0.11, -0.31,  0.24),
  lower     = c( 0.05, -0.61, -0.04, -0.52,  0.08),
  upper     = c( 0.31, -0.23,  0.26, -0.10,  0.40)
)

forrest(
  dat,
  estimate = "estimate",
  lower    = "lower",
  upper    = "upper",
  label    = "predictor",
  xlab     = "Regression coefficient (95% CI)"
)

title: Introduction to forrest
section: Section headers from a grouping column
text:
Section headers from a grouping column
When section names a column, forrest() inserts a bold header row wherever that column’s value changes, indents the labels beneath it, and adds a blank row after each section. Rows stay in the order they have in the data, so sort the data first if the sections should appear in a particular order.

sub_dat <- data.frame(
  subgroup = c("Sex",    "Sex",
               "Age group", "Age group", "Age group"),
  label    = c("Female", "Male",
               "30–49 years", "50–69 years", "70+ years"),
  estimate = c(-0.38,  0.12,  0.22, -0.15, -0.41),
  lower    = c(-0.58, -0.08,  0.02, -0.38, -0.66),
  upper    = c(-0.18,  0.32,  0.42,  0.08, -0.16)
)

forrest(
  sub_dat,
  estimate = "estimate",
  lower    = "lower",
  upper    = "upper",
  label    = "label",
  section  = "subgroup",
  xlab     = "Regression coefficient (95% CI)",
  header   = "Subgroup"
)








section_indent = FALSE turns off the indentation and section_spacer = FALSE removes the blank row after each section.

Two levels of headers
Adding subsection gives a second level: indented sub-headers wherever the subsection value changes within a section.

nested_dat <- data.frame(
  domain    = c(
    "Physical environment", "Physical environment", "Physical environment",
    "Physical environment", "Physical environment",
    "Social environment",   "Social environment",
    "Social environment",   "Social environment"
  ),
  type      = c(
    "Air quality", "Air quality",
    "Urban form",  "Urban form",  "Urban form",
    "Support",     "Support",
    "Deprivation", "Deprivation"
  ),
  predictor = c(
    "PM2.5 (per 10 μg/m³)", "NO2 (per 10 ppb)",
    "Green space (%)", "Walkability", "Noise (per 10 dB)",
    "Social cohesion", "Social isolation",
    "Area deprivation", "Employment rate"
  ),
  estimate  = c(-0.18,  0.12, -0.22,  0.15, -0.08,
                -0.11,  0.09,  0.05, -0.03),
  lower     = c(-0.38, -0.08, -0.42, -0.05, -0.28,
                -0.31, -0.09, -0.12, -0.20),
  upper     = c( 0.02,  0.32, -0.02,  0.35,  0.12,
                 0.09,  0.27,  0.22,  0.14)
)

forrest(
  nested_dat,
  estimate   = "estimate",
  lower      = "lower",
  upper      = "upper",
  label      = "predictor",
  section    = "domain",
  subsection = "type",
  xlab       = "Mean difference in SBP (mmHg, 95% CI)"
)

title: Introduction to forrest
text:
Summary estimates
Rows where the is_summary column is TRUE are drawn as filled diamonds spanning the confidence interval, the usual mark for a pooled or overall estimate.

sex_dat <- data.frame(
  label    = c("Female", "Male", "Overall"),
  estimate = c(-0.42, -0.29, -0.36),
  lower    = c(-0.61, -0.48, -0.50),
  upper    = c(-0.23, -0.10, -0.22),
  is_sum   = c(FALSE, FALSE, TRUE)
)

forrest(
  sex_dat,
  estimate   = "estimate",
  lower      = "lower",
  upper      = "upper",
  label      = "label",
  is_summary = "is_sum",
  xlab       = "Regression coefficient (95% CI)",
  title      = "Association of physical activity with SBP, by sex"
)

title: Introduction to forrest
text:
Group colours
A group column colours each row by its value and adds a legend. The default palette is Okabe-Ito, which stays distinguishable under the common forms of colour blindness. To choose the colours yourself, pass col, either as an unnamed vector used in order of appearance or as a vector named by group level.

grp_dat <- data.frame(
  predictor = c("Air pollution (PM2.5)", "Noise exposure",
                "Green space access", "Walkability index",
                "Food environment",
                "Social cohesion", "Social isolation",
                "Area deprivation", "Neighbourhood safety",
                "Employment rate"),
  domain    = rep(c("Physical environment", "Social environment"),
                  each = 5),
  estimate  = c(-0.18,  0.12, -0.22,  0.15, -0.08,
                 0.05, -0.03,  0.09, -0.11,  0.14),
  lower     = c(-0.38, -0.08, -0.42, -0.05, -0.28,
                -0.12, -0.20, -0.09, -0.31, -0.04),
  upper     = c( 0.02,  0.32, -0.02,  0.35,  0.12,
                 0.22,  0.14,  0.27,  0.09,  0.32)
)

forrest(
  grp_dat,
  estimate = "estimate",
  lower    = "lower",
  upper    = "upper",
  label    = "predictor",
  group    = "domain",
  xlab     = "Mean difference in SBP (mmHg, 95% CI)"
)

title: Introduction to forrest
text:
Several estimates per row
With dodge = TRUE, consecutive rows that share a label value are drawn as one band: their intervals are offset vertically around the band’s centre and the label appears once. Pair it with group so the reader can tell the series apart.

dodge_dat <- data.frame(
  exposure = rep(
    c("PM2.5 (per 10 μg/m³)", "NO2 (per 10 ppb)",
      "Noise (per 10 dB)", "Green space (%)", "Walkability"),
    each = 2
  ),
  period   = rep(c("Childhood", "Adulthood"), 5),
  estimate = c(
     0.14, -0.05,  0.08,  0.12, -0.19, -0.06,  0.11, -0.03,  0.07,  0.10
  ),
  lower    = c(
    -0.10, -0.26, -0.09, -0.08, -0.40, -0.25, -0.05, -0.12, -0.14, -0.09
  ),
  upper    = c(
     0.38,  0.16,  0.25,  0.32,  0.02,  0.13,  0.27,  0.06,  0.28,  0.29
  )
)

forrest(
  dodge_dat,
  estimate = "estimate",
  lower    = "lower",
  upper    = "upper",
  label    = "exposure",
  group    = "period",
  dodge    = TRUE,
  header   = "Environmental exposure",
  xlab     = "Mean difference in SBP (mmHg, 95% CI)"
)








A number instead of TRUE sets the distance between neighbouring intervals in a band, in units of one row; TRUE means 0.25. Section and subsection headers and spacer rows are never merged into a band.

One text column per series
By default each text column in cols prints a value beside every interval, at that interval’s offset position. With cols_by_group = TRUE, each text column instead prints one value per band, at the band’s centre: the first non-empty value among the band’s rows. Giving each series its own column, filled only on that series’ rows, produces a wide table with one row per label and one column per series.

dodge_dat$est_ci     <- sprintf("%.2f (%.2f, %.2f)",
                                dodge_dat$estimate,
                                dodge_dat$lower,
                                dodge_dat$upper)
dodge_dat$text_child <- ifelse(
  dodge_dat$period == "Childhood", dodge_dat$est_ci, ""
)
dodge_dat$text_adult <- ifelse(
  dodge_dat$period == "Adulthood", dodge_dat$est_ci, ""
)

forrest(
  dodge_dat,
  estimate      = "estimate",
  lower         = "lower",
  upper         = "upper",
  label         = "exposure",
  group         = "period",
  dodge         = TRUE,
  cols_by_group = TRUE,
  cols          = c("Childhood (95% CI)" = "text_child",
                    "Adulthood (95% CI)" = "text_adult"),
  widths        = c(2.8, 3.5, 2.2, 2.2),
  header        = "Environmental exposure",
  xlab          = "Mean difference in SBP (mmHg, 95% CI)"
)

title: Introduction to forrest
text:
Point shapes
A shape column gives each of its values a different point character and adds a second legend. Combined with group and dodge, a single band can then encode two variables, here period by colour and sex by shape.

shape_dat <- data.frame(
  exposure = rep(
    c("PM2.5 (per 10 μg/m³)", "NO2 (per 10 ppb)",
      "Noise (per 10 dB)", "Green space (%)", "Walkability"),
    each = 4
  ),
  period   = rep(rep(c("Childhood", "Adulthood"), each = 2), 5),
  sex      = rep(c("Female", "Male"), 10),
  estimate = c(
     0.22, -0.08, -0.10,  0.18,
     0.11,  0.05,  0.00,  0.14,
    -0.31,  0.06, -0.09, -0.02,
     0.08,  0.12, -0.04,  0.03,
     0.17, -0.06,  0.22,  0.01
  ),
  lower    = c(
    -0.20, -0.38, -0.28, -0.14,
    -0.12, -0.22, -0.22, -0.14,
    -0.56, -0.24, -0.38, -0.30,
    -0.18, -0.14, -0.22, -0.15,
    -0.09, -0.38, -0.04, -0.27
  ),
  upper    = c(
     0.64,  0.22,  0.08,  0.50,
     0.34,  0.32,  0.22,  0.42,
    -0.06,  0.36,  0.20,  0.26,
     0.34,  0.38,  0.14,  0.21,
     0.43,  0.26,  0.48,  0.29
  )
)

forrest(
  shape_dat,
  estimate = "estimate",
  lower    = "lower",
  upper    = "upper",
  label    = "exposure",
  group    = "period",
  shape    = "sex",
  dodge    = TRUE,
  xlab     = "Mean difference in SBP (mmHg, 95% CI)"
)








The shape legend sits at legend_shape_pos, "bottomright" by default, and legend_shape_pos = NULL removes it. legend_pos does the same for the colour legend.

title: Introduction to forrest
text:
Text columns
cols adds text columns to the right of the plot. It is a named character vector: each name is a column header and each value is the name of a column in data. Format the text yourself, for instance with sprintf(), so that it shows exactly the digits you want. widths sets the relative widths of the label panel, the plot and each text column.

tc_dat <- data.frame(
  predictor = c("Age (per 10 y)", "Female sex", "BMI (per 5 kg/m²)",
                "Current smoker", "Physically active"),
  estimate  = c( 0.18, -0.42,  0.11, -0.31,  0.24),
  lower     = c( 0.05, -0.61, -0.04, -0.52,  0.08),
  upper     = c( 0.31, -0.23,  0.26, -0.10,  0.40),
  coef_ci   = c(
    " 0.18 ( 0.05,  0.31)",
    "-0.42 (-0.61, -0.23)",
    " 0.11 (-0.04,  0.26)",
    "-0.31 (-0.52, -0.10)",
    " 0.24 ( 0.08,  0.40)"
  ),
  pval = c("0.006", "<0.001", "0.148", "0.003", "0.009")
)

forrest(
  tc_dat,
  estimate = "estimate",
  lower    = "lower",
  upper    = "upper",
  label    = "predictor",
  header   = "Predictor",
  cols     = c("Coef (95% CI)" = "coef_ci", "P-value" = "pval"),
  widths   = c(2.8, 4, 2.5, 1.2),
  xlab     = "Regression coefficient (95% CI)"
)









Values in section header rows
Text columns are empty on the header rows that section inserts. section_cols fills chosen text columns on those rows with a section-level value. Its names must be names of cols, and its values are columns in data; on each header row, the named text column shows the first non-empty value of that data column within the section. subsection_cols does the same for subsection headers. Here each row shows its own sample size and each header shows the section’s total.

sc_dat <- data.frame(
  subgroup  = c("Sex",    "Sex",   "Age group", "Age group", "Age group"),
  label     = c("Female", "Male",  "30–49 y", "50–69 y", "70+ y"),
  estimate  = c(-0.38,  0.12,  0.22, -0.15, -0.41),
  lower     = c(-0.58, -0.08,  0.02, -0.38, -0.66),
  upper     = c(-0.18,  0.32,  0.42,  0.08, -0.16),
  coef_ci   = c(
    "-0.38 (-0.58, -0.18)",
    " 0.12 (-0.08,  0.32)",
    " 0.22 ( 0.02,  0.42)",
    "-0.15 (-0.38,  0.08)",
    "-0.41 (-0.66, -0.16)"
  ),
  n_text    = c("1,204", "1,096", "702", "958", "640"),
  n_section = c("2,300", "", "2,300", "", "")
)

forrest(
  sc_dat,
  estimate     = "estimate",
  lower        = "lower",
  upper        = "upper",
  label        = "label",
  section      = "subgroup",
  section_cols = c("N" = "n_section"),
  header       = "Subgroup",
  cols         = c("Coef (95% CI)" = "coef_ci", "N" = "n_text"),
  widths       = c(2.5, 4, 2.5, 1.2),
  xlab         = "Regression coefficient (95% CI)"
)

title: Introduction to forrest
text:
Row stripes
stripe = TRUE shades every other row, which helps the eye follow a row across a wide plot.

stripe_dat <- data.frame(
  label    = c(
    "Age (per 10 y)", "Female sex", "BMI (per 5 kg/m²)",
    "Current smoker", "Physically active",
    "Alcohol intake", "Sleep duration", "Depressive symptoms"
  ),
  estimate = c( 0.42, -0.18,  0.31, -0.07,  0.25, -0.12,  0.19, -0.34),
  lower    = c( 0.22, -0.38,  0.12, -0.24,  0.06, -0.30,  0.01, -0.52),
  upper    = c( 0.62,  0.02,  0.50,  0.10,  0.44,  0.06,  0.37, -0.16)
)

forrest(
  stripe_dat,
  estimate = "estimate",
  lower    = "lower",
  upper    = "upper",
  label    = "label",
  stripe   = TRUE,
  xlab     = "Regression coefficient (95% CI)"
)

title: Introduction to forrest
text:
Themes
theme takes the name of a built-in theme ("default", "minimal" or "classic") or a named list that overrides individual keys of the default theme. The keys are grid_col, grid_lty and grid_lwd for the horizontal gridlines, ref_col and ref_lty for the reference line, and stripe_col for striped rows.

theme_dat <- data.frame(
  predictor = c("Age (per 10 y)", "Female sex", "BMI (per 5 kg/m²)"),
  estimate  = c( 0.18, -0.42,  0.11),
  lower     = c( 0.05, -0.61, -0.04),
  upper     = c( 0.31, -0.23,  0.26)
)

# Lighter gridlines and a softer reference line
forrest(
  theme_dat,
  estimate = "estimate",
  lower    = "lower",
  upper    = "upper",
  label    = "predictor",
  theme    = "minimal",
  title    = 'theme = "minimal"',
  xlab     = "Coefficient (95% CI)"
)









# Dotted gridlines and a solid black reference line
forrest(
  theme_dat,
  estimate = "estimate",
  lower    = "lower",
  upper    = "upper",
  label    = "predictor",
  theme    = "classic",
  title    = 'theme = "classic"',
  xlab     = "Coefficient (95% CI)"
)









forrest(
  theme_dat,
  estimate = "estimate",
  lower    = "lower",
  upper    = "upper",
  label    = "predictor",
  theme    = list(ref_col = "#e63946", ref_lty = 1L, grid_col = "#eeeeee"),
  title    = "Custom theme (red reference line)",
  xlab     = "Coefficient (95% CI)"
)








Graphical parameters that forrest() does not name, such as cex.axis and cex.lab, are passed through ... to the call that sets up the plot region.

title: Introduction to forrest
text:
Saving plots
save_forrest() writes a plot to PDF, PNG, SVG or TIFF, choosing the device from the file extension. It takes a function with no arguments that draws the plot, so the device is opened before drawing starts and closed even if drawing fails. dpi sets the resolution of PNG and TIFF files.

save_forrest(
  file   = "my_forest_plot.pdf",
  plot   = function() {
    forrest(
      dat,
      estimate = "estimate",
      lower    = "lower",
      upper    = "upper",
      label    = "predictor",
      xlab     = "Regression coefficient (95% CI)"
    )
  },
  width  = 8,
  height = 5
)

title: Forest plots for meta-analyses
text:
In a meta-analysis forest plot each row is one study, the size of its marker reflects the study’s weight, and a diamond at the bottom shows the pooled estimate. This vignette builds that plot and its common variants for an invented meta-analysis of long-term exposure to fine particulate matter (PM2.5) and incident hypertension. The study names and numbers are made up.
forrest() only draws; it does not pool. Compute the pooled estimates with a meta-analysis package such as metafor or meta, or by hand as below, and pass the results in as rows.

title: Forest plots for meta-analyses
text:
Data
Each study contributes a log odds ratio per 10 μg/m³ of PM2.5 and its standard error, chosen to scatter around a log odds ratio of 0.08. The pooled row is a fixed-effect (inverse-variance) estimate.

meta_dat <- data.frame(
  study    = c(
    "Anderson et al. (2014)",
    "Bauer et al. (2015)",
    "Chen et al. (2016)",
    "Di et al. (2017)",
    "Evans et al. (2018)",
    "Fuentes et al. (2019)",
    "Garcia et al. (2020)",
    "Hart et al. (2021)",
    "Ibrahim et al. (2022)",
    "Jensen et al. (2023)"
  ),
  region   = c(
    "North America", "Europe", "Asia", "North America", "Europe",
    "Latin America", "Europe", "North America", "Asia", "Europe"
  ),
  n        = c(4520, 2810, 8340, 12600, 3950, 1870, 5430, 9100, 6780, 3210),
  events   = c( 612,  390, 1120,  1950,  540,  255,  770, 1380, 980,  450),
  log_or   = c(0.062, 0.091, 0.078, 0.095, 0.055, 0.110, 0.083,
               0.072, 0.088, 0.068),
  se       = c(0.028, 0.035, 0.022, 0.019, 0.031, 0.042, 0.026,
               0.021, 0.024, 0.033),
  is_sum   = FALSE
)

# Odds ratios and 95% CIs on the natural scale
meta_dat$or    <- exp(meta_dat$log_or)
meta_dat$lower <- exp(meta_dat$log_or - 1.96 * meta_dat$se)
meta_dat$upper <- exp(meta_dat$log_or + 1.96 * meta_dat$se)

# Inverse-variance weights
meta_dat$weight <- 1 / meta_dat$se^2

pooled_log_or <- with(meta_dat, sum(weight * log_or) / sum(weight))
pooled_se     <- sqrt(1 / sum(meta_dat$weight))

pooled_row <- data.frame(
  study    = "Pooled (fixed-effect)",
  region   = NA_character_,
  n        = sum(meta_dat$n),
  events   = sum(meta_dat$events),
  log_or   = pooled_log_or,
  se       = pooled_se,
  or       = exp(pooled_log_or),
  lower    = exp(pooled_log_or - 1.96 * pooled_se),
  upper    = exp(pooled_log_or + 1.96 * pooled_se),
  weight   = NA_real_,
  is_sum   = TRUE
)
meta_all <- rbind(meta_dat, pooled_row)

# Text for the right-hand columns
meta_all$or_text     <- sprintf("%.2f (%.2f–%.2f)",
                                meta_all$or, meta_all$lower, meta_all$upper)
meta_all$n_text      <- formatC(meta_all$n,      format = "d", big.mark = ",")
meta_all$events_text <- formatC(meta_all$events, format = "d", big.mark = ",")

title: Forest plots for meta-analyses
text:
Basic plot
Odds ratios belong on a log axis, where an odds ratio of 2 and one of 0.5 sit at the same distance from 1. With log_scale = TRUE the reference line moves to 1 by default. weight scales the marker so that its area is proportional to the study’s weight, and is_summary turns the pooled row into a diamond.

forrest(
  meta_all,
  estimate   = "or",
  lower      = "lower",
  upper      = "upper",
  label      = "study",
  is_summary = "is_sum",
  weight     = "weight",
  log_scale  = TRUE,
  xlab       = "OR for hypertension per 10 μg/m³ PM2.5 (95% CI)"
)

title: Forest plots for meta-analyses
text:
Text columns
Published meta-analysis plots usually print the sample size, event count and estimate beside each study. cols adds these as text columns and header labels the study column.

forrest(
  meta_all,
  estimate   = "or",
  lower      = "lower",
  upper      = "upper",
  label      = "study",
  is_summary = "is_sum",
  weight     = "weight",
  log_scale  = TRUE,
  header     = "Study",
  cols       = c(
    "N"            = "n_text",
    "Events"       = "events_text",
    "OR (95% CI)"  = "or_text"
  ),
  widths     = c(3.5, 3.5, 1.2, 1.2, 2.2),
  xlab       = "OR for hypertension per 10 μg/m³ PM2.5 (95% CI)"
)

title: Forest plots for meta-analyses
text:
Colour by region
Colouring the study rows by region shows at a glance whether estimates cluster geographically. The pooled row is left out here because it belongs to no region.

study_dat <- meta_all[!meta_all$is_sum, ]

forrest(
  study_dat,
  estimate   = "or",
  lower      = "lower",
  upper      = "upper",
  label      = "study",
  group      = "region",
  log_scale  = TRUE,
  xlab       = "OR for hypertension per 10 μg/m³ PM2.5 (95% CI)"
)

title: Forest plots for meta-analyses
text:
Subgroup analysis by region
For a formal subgroup analysis, each region gets its own header, its studies and its own pooled diamond. section = "region" inserts the headers, so the data only need the study rows and one pooled row per region, sorted by region.

# Fixed-effect pooled row for one region
pool_region <- function(dat, region_label) {
  w   <- 1 / dat$se^2
  lp  <- sum(w * dat$log_or) / sum(w)
  se  <- sqrt(1 / sum(w))
  data.frame(
    study    = sprintf("%s (pooled)", region_label),
    region   = region_label,
    n        = sum(dat$n),
    events   = sum(dat$events),
    log_or   = lp,
    se       = se,
    or       = exp(lp),
    lower    = exp(lp - 1.96 * se),
    upper    = exp(lp + 1.96 * se),
    weight   = sum(w),
    is_sum   = TRUE
  )
}

regions    <- c("Asia", "Europe", "Latin America", "North America")
structured <- do.call(rbind, lapply(regions, function(r) {
  sub <- meta_dat[meta_dat$region == r, ]
  rbind(sub, pool_region(sub, r))
}))

structured$or_text <- sprintf(
  "%.2f (%.2f–%.2f)",
  structured$or, structured$lower, structured$upper
)

forrest(
  structured,
  estimate   = "or",
  lower      = "lower",
  upper      = "upper",
  label      = "study",
  section    = "region",
  is_summary = "is_sum",
  weight     = "weight",
  log_scale  = TRUE,
  header     = "Study",
  cols       = c("OR (95% CI)" = "or_text"),
  widths     = c(4, 3.5, 2.5),
  stripe     = TRUE,
  xlab       = "OR for hypertension per 10 μg/m³ PM2.5 (95% CI)"
)








Latin America has a single study, so its pooled estimate equals that study’s estimate.

title: Forest plots for meta-analyses
section: Several exposures in the same studies
text:
Several exposures in the same studies
When the same studies report several exposures, one band per study with one interval per exposure lets the reader compare exposures within a study. The data have one row per study and exposure, sorted by study; group colours the exposures and dodge = TRUE offsets them within each band.

set.seed(99)
studies6 <- c("Anderson (2018)", "Bauer (2019)", "Chen (2020)",
              "Di (2021)", "Evans (2022)", "Fuentes (2023)")

make_exp <- function(true_lor, n = 6) {
  se  <- runif(n, 0.025, 0.045)
  lor <- rnorm(n, true_lor, 0.02)
  data.frame(
    or    = exp(lor),
    lower = exp(lor - 1.96 * se),
    upper = exp(lor + 1.96 * se)
  )
}

multi_exp <- cbind(
  data.frame(
    study    = rep(studies6, 3),
    exposure = rep(c("PM2.5", "NO2", "Noise"), each = 6)
  ),
  rbind(make_exp(0.08), make_exp(0.05), make_exp(0.03))
)
multi_exp <- multi_exp[order(match(multi_exp$study, studies6)), ]

forrest(
  multi_exp,
  estimate   = "or",
  lower      = "lower",
  upper      = "upper",
  label      = "study",
  group      = "exposure",
  dodge      = TRUE,
  log_scale  = TRUE,
  header     = "Study",
  xlab       = "OR for hypertension (95% CI)"
)

title: forrest
text:
forrest draws publication-ready forest plots from any data frame with one row per estimate and columns for the point estimate and its confidence limits: regression coefficients, subgroup estimates, studies in a meta-analysis, exposure categories. Its only dependency is tinyplot.
A single function, forrest(), covers the layouts these tables need:

bold section headers, and optionally a second level of sub-headers, generated from grouping columns, so the data never need hand-inserted blank rows;
diamonds for pooled or overall estimates, and label-only rows for reference categories;
colours and point shapes mapped from columns, with legends, and several estimates per row offset vertically so their intervals do not overlap;
formatted text columns beside the plot, such as estimates with confidence intervals or p-values;
a log axis for ratio measures, marker sizes scaled by study weight, row stripes, three themes, and arrows where an interval runs past the axis limits.

save_forrest() writes the plot to PDF, PNG, SVG or TIFF. Both functions accept data frames, tibbles and data.tables.


install.packages("forrest")

# Development version from GitHub:
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("lorenzoFabbri/forrest")





The minimal call names three columns: estimate, lower and upper. Here each exposure class has two estimates, one per period; group colours them and dodge = TRUE draws both within the exposure’s row. The introduction shows every feature in turn.
library(forrest)

# Two estimates per exposure (e.g., two time windows)
periods <- data.frame(
  exposure = rep(c("Metals", "OPPs", "PFAS", "Phenols", "Phthalates"), each = 2),
  period   = rep(c("Pregnancy", "Childhood"), 5),
  est      = c( 0.03, -0.04, -0.03,  0.04, -0.17, -0.02,  0.10, -0.02,  0.07,  0.10),
  lo       = c(-0.25, -0.26, -0.19, -0.12, -0.40, -0.24, -0.06, -0.10, -0.15, -0.08),
  hi       = c( 0.30,  0.19,  0.13,  0.21,  0.06,  0.19,  0.26,  0.07,  0.29,  0.28)
)

forrest(
  periods,
  estimate = "est",
  lower    = "lo",
  upper    = "hi",
  label    = "exposure",
  group    = "period",
  dodge    = TRUE,
  header   = "Exposure class",
  xlab     = "Coefficient (95% CI)"
)




With log_scale = TRUE the axis is logarithmic and the reference line moves to 1. is_summary draws the pooled row as a diamond, and weight scales each study’s marker by its inverse-variance weight. The meta-analysis vignette adds subgroup analyses and several exposures per study.

             "Davis 2020", "Evans 2021", "Pooled"),
  est    = c(1.45, 0.88, 1.21, 1.07, 0.95, 1.09),

The regression vignette covers adjustment sets, multiple outcomes, exposure categories, and average treatment effects by g-computation and inverse probability weighting.
set.seed(1)

  sbp    = 120 + rnorm(n, sd = 15),
  age    = runif(n, 30, 70),
  female = rbinom(n, 1, 0.5),
  bmi    = rnorm(n, 26, 4),
  smoker = rbinom(n, 1, 0.2)
)

           0.5 * dat$bmi - 2 * dat$smoker + rnorm(n, sd = 6)

  "%.2f (%.2f, %.2f)",
  coefs$estimate, coefs$conf.low, coefs$conf.high

forrest(
  coefs,
  estimate = "estimate",
  lower    = "conf.low",
  upper    = "conf.high",
  label    = "term",
  header   = "Predictor",
  cols     = c("Coef (95% CI)" = "coef_ci"),
  widths   = c(3, 4, 2.5),
  xlab     = "Regression coefficient (95% CI)",

title: forrest 0.4.0
text:
When group or shape named the same column as label and section was set, the legend listed the section names and indented labels as group levels. Group and shape values are now read before section rows are inserted, and inserted rows no longer add an NA entry to either legend.
dodge = TRUE failed with “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed” when a label was NA. Missing labels are now drawn as blank text.
On a log axis, the arrows that mark an interval running past xlim had shafts of very different lengths at the two ends of the axis. Their length is now 2% of the axis width on both sides.
col was ignored for the legend when group was also set, and a per-row col vector lost its alignment with the rows once section inserted header rows. With group, col now gives one colour per group level, by name or in order; without group, it must have length 1 or one entry per row.
section_cols and subsection_cols wrote the header value into their source column rather than into the column shown under the given header, so the header cell stayed empty whenever the two columns differed.
Panel headers set by header and the names of cols overlapped the first row in plots with many rows; they now sit a fixed distance above the plot region.
With dodge, summary diamonds in the same row overlapped each other. Their height is now capped at 0.45 times the dodge offset.
A weight column with no usable values produced a warning from max(). Marker sizes now fall back to cex.





With log_scale = TRUE, ref_line now defaults to 1 instead of 0, which cannot be drawn on a log axis. An explicit ref_line of 0 or less gives a warning and no line.
log_scale = TRUE with a non-positive estimate, confidence limit or xlim is now an error that explains the cause, instead of a failure inside the plotting code.
Column arguments must be single strings, theme lists may use only the six documented keys, and save_forrest() checks that plot is a function. Each case now stops with a message naming the argument.





The theme keys are listed in ?forrest, and the documentation of ref_label, ref_line and col matches what they do.

title: forrest 0.4.0
text:
New features

forrest() gains a dodge argument (logical or positive numeric, default FALSE). When set, consecutive rows that share the same label value are grouped together and their confidence intervals are drawn with a small vertical offset so they do not overlap. The shared label is displayed once at the centre of the group. Designed to be used with group (for colour) and/or shape (for point character) to visually distinguish the overlaid series. A numeric value controls the offset directly; TRUE uses a default of 0.25 y-axis units.
forrest() gains a shape argument (column name string, default NULL). When provided, different values of the column are rendered with different point characters from a built-in set (circle, triangle, square, diamond, …), and a shape legend is drawn automatically. Most useful in combination with group to encode two categorical dimensions simultaneously (e.g. colour = time period, shape = sex).
forrest() gains a legend_shape_pos argument (default "bottomright") to control the position of the shape legend independently of legend_pos.
forrest() gains a cols_by_group argument (default FALSE). When TRUE and dodge is active, each text column in cols is collapsed to one value per label group displayed at the group centre y position. This produces a wide-format text table — one row per label, one column per condition — as commonly seen in multi-period epidemiology papers (vs. the default behaviour of stacking text at each individual row’s dodged y position).

title: forrest
text:
Draws a publication-ready forest plot from a data frame. Each row represents one estimate — a study, a predictor, a model, a subgroup, or any other unit of analysis.



forrest(
  data,
  estimate,
  lower,
  upper,
  label = NULL,
  group = NULL,
  is_summary = NULL,
  weight = NULL,
  section = NULL,
  subsection = NULL,
  section_indent = TRUE,
  section_spacer = TRUE,
  section_cols = NULL,
  subsection_cols = NULL,
  ref_label = FALSE,
  ref_line = 0,
  log_scale = FALSE,
  xlim = NULL,
  xlab = "Estimate (95% CI)",
  title = NULL,
  header = NULL,
  cols = NULL,
  widths = NULL,
  stripe = FALSE,
  dodge = FALSE,
  pch = 15,
  shape = NULL,
  lwd = 2,
  cex = 1,
  col = NULL,
  cols_by_group = FALSE,
  legend_pos = "topright",
  legend_shape_pos = "bottomright",
  theme = "default",
  ...
)







data


A data frame, tibble, or data.table.




estimate


Column name (string) for point estimates.




lower


Column name (string) for lower confidence interval bounds.




upper


Column name (string) for upper confidence interval bounds.




label


Column name (string) for row labels displayed on the y-axis or in the left text panel. If NULL, row numbers are used.




group


Column name (string) for a grouping variable. Rows that share a group value receive the same colour, and a legend is drawn automatically.




is_summary


Column name (string) of a logical vector. Rows where this is TRUE are drawn as filled diamonds (e.g. pooled or overall estimates) rather than squares with whiskers.




weight


Column name (string) of numeric row weights. When provided, point size scales as cex * sqrt(weight / max(weight)), so rows with larger weights appear with a bigger marker. Weights for summary rows are ignored (diamond size is fixed by cex).




section


Column name (string) for a grouping variable that determines section structure. Whenever the value of this column changes (run-length boundary), a bold section header row is automatically inserted before the group. Row order is preserved; no automatic sorting is applied. See also section_indent, section_spacer, and section_cols.




subsection


Column name (string) for a second-level grouping variable. Requires section. Inserts indented sub-headers beneath each section header. See also subsection_cols.




section_indent


Logical. If TRUE (default), label values of data rows within a section are automatically indented by two spaces (four spaces for rows within a subsection).




section_spacer


Logical. If TRUE (default), a blank spacer row is appended after the last row of each section.




section_cols


Named character vector. Names must be a subset of the names of cols. Values are column names in data; on each section’s header row, the text column with that name shows the first non-empty value of the data column within the section. Text columns not listed are empty on header rows. Use this to show section-level summaries, such as the number of studies, beside the section header.




subsection_cols


Like section_cols but for subsection header rows.




ref_label


Logical. When TRUE, reference-category rows (rows of data whose estimate is NA, as opposed to the header rows that section inserts) have ” (Ref.)“ appended to their label. Default is FALSE.




ref_line


Numeric. Position of the vertical reference line: 0 for differences, 1 for ratio measures. Set to NULL to suppress. Defaults to 0, or to 1 when log_scale = TRUE.




log_scale


Logical. If TRUE, the x-axis is drawn on a log scale, for odds ratios, hazard ratios or risk ratios supplied on the natural (not log) scale. All estimates and confidence limits must then be positive. Default is FALSE.




xlim


Numeric vector of length 2 giving x-axis limits. Computed from the data when NULL (default). Confidence intervals that extend beyond xlim are clipped at the axis boundary and an arrow is drawn to indicate truncation.




xlab


Label for the x-axis. Default is “Estimate (95% CI)”.




title


Plot title. Default is NULL (no title).




header


Optional header string placed above the label column. When cols is provided this appears above the left text panel; otherwise it is drawn above the topmost row on the y-axis.




cols


Named character vector specifying extra text columns to display to the right of the plot. Names become column headers; values are column names in data, for example cols = c(“OR (95% CI)” = “or_ci”).




widths


Numeric vector of relative panel widths. When cols is NULL, ignored. Otherwise, length must equal 2 + length(cols): label panel, plot panel, then one entry per extra column. Sensible defaults are chosen automatically.




stripe


Logical. If TRUE, alternate rows are shaded with a light grey background to improve readability. Default is FALSE.




dodge


Logical or positive numeric. When TRUE (or a positive number), consecutive rows that share the same label value are grouped together and their confidence intervals are drawn with a small vertical offset so that they do not overlap. The shared label is displayed once at the centre of the group. Use together with group (for colour) and/or shape (for point characters) to distinguish the overlaid series. A numeric value sets the offset between rows in a group directly (in y-axis units); TRUE uses a default of 0.25. Default is FALSE.




pch


Point character for non-summary rows. Default is 15 (filled square). When shape is provided, pch is used only as a fallback for rows whose shape value is NA.




shape


Column name (string) for a shape variable. When provided, different values of the column are rendered with different point characters and a shape legend is drawn. Use together with group to distinguish two categorical dimensions simultaneously (e.g. colour = time period, shape = sex).




lwd


Line width for confidence interval whiskers. Default is 2.




cex


Point size multiplier. Default is 1.




col


Colours. With group, one colour per group level: a named vector is matched to the levels by name, and an unnamed one is recycled over the levels in order of appearance. Without group, a single colour or one colour per row of data. When NULL (default), groups take the Okabe-Ito colorblind-safe palette and ungrouped rows are drawn in near-black.




cols_by_group


Logical. Relevant only when dodge is active. When TRUE, each text column in cols is collapsed to one value per label group: the first non-empty entry within the group is displayed at the group centre y position. This produces a wide-format text table with one row per label and one column per condition. Populate each text column so that the value is non-empty only for the matching condition row and empty (““) for all others; forrest() picks up the right value automatically. When FALSE (default), text values are drawn at each individual row’s dodged y position, keeping them aligned with their CI whiskers.

Position of the colour legend when group is supplied. Passed to legend(). Use NULL to suppress. Default is “topright”.




legend_shape_pos


Position of the shape legend when shape is supplied. Passed to legend(). Use NULL to suppress. Default is “bottomright”.




theme


Visual theme: one of “default”, “minimal” or “classic”, or a named list that overrides individual style keys of the default theme. The keys are grid_col, grid_lty and grid_lwd (horizontal gridlines), ref_col and ref_lty (reference line), and stripe_col (background of striped rows). Default is “default”.




…


Graphical parameters forwarded to the internal tinyplot call (e.g. cex.axis, cex.lab).






Rows with NA estimates are treated as reference-category rows: they produce no point or confidence interval, and their label is rendered in regular (non-bold) font.   predictor = c("Age (per 10 y)", "Female sex",

  estimate  = c(0.42, -0.38,  0.19, -0.31),
  lower     = c(0.22, -0.56, -0.02, -0.51),
  upper     = c(0.62, -0.20,  0.40, -0.11)
)
forrest(dat,
  estimate = "estimate",
  lower    = "lower",
  upper    = "upper",
  label    = "predictor",
  xlab     = "Regression coefficient (95% CI)"
)







# Section headers from a grouping column
dat2 <- data.frame(
  domain    = c("Lifestyle", "Lifestyle", "Clinical", "Clinical"),
  predictor = c("Physical activity", "Diet quality",
                "BMI (per 5 kg/m\u00b2)", "Systolic BP (per 10 mmHg)"),
  estimate  = c(-0.31, -0.18,  0.19,  0.25),
  lower     = c(-0.51, -0.36, -0.02,  0.08),
  upper     = c(-0.11, -0.00,  0.40,  0.42)

  estimate  = "estimate",
  lower     = "lower",
  upper     = "upper",
  label     = "predictor",
  section   = "domain",
  xlab      = "Regression coefficient (95% CI)"
)

text:
Writes the plot produced by forrest() (or any base-R plotting code) to a file. The graphics device is inferred from the file extension.



save_forrest(file, plot, width = 7, height = 5, dpi = 300, bg = "white")

Output file path. Supported extensions: .pdf, .png, .svg, .tiff.

A zero-argument function whose body calls forrest(). Evaluated inside the open graphics device.




width

    dat,
    estimate = "estimate",

    label    = "label",
    xlab     = "Regression coefficient (95% CI)"

text: This vignette follows one data set through forrest(), calling the internal helpers directly to show what each step produces before anything is drawn. The helpers are not exported and are reached with :::; their interfaces may change between releases.

title: How forrest works
text:
Design
forrest() is the only plotting function, and every layout is reached through its arguments, which name columns of the data as strings. The data stay tidy, one row per estimate. Visual structure such as section headers, indentation and blank rows is derived from grouping columns at draw time, so it never has to be written into the data.
All drawing uses base R graphics. The one dependency, tinyplot, sets up the plot region, so the axes and fonts follow tinyplot’s theming.

title: How forrest works
text:
Example data
Seven studies from three regions, with odds ratios, weights and a formatted text column:

or    <- c(1.081, 1.092, 1.095, 1.057, 1.086, 1.070, 1.116)
lower <- c(1.038, 1.052, 1.058, 1.019, 1.050, 1.036, 1.063)
upper <- c(1.126, 1.134, 1.134, 1.096, 1.123, 1.105, 1.171)

meta <- data.frame(
  study   = c("Chen (2016)", "Ibrahim (2022)",
              "Bauer (2015)", "Evans (2018)", "Garcia (2020)", "Jensen (2023)",
              "Fuentes (2019)"),
  region  = c("Asia", "Asia",
              "Europe", "Europe", "Europe", "Europe",
              "Latin America"),
  or      = or,
  lower   = lower,
  upper   = upper,
  weight  = c(2065, 1736, 816, 1041, 1479, 918, 567),
  is_sum  = FALSE,
  or_text = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f–%.2f)", or, lower, upper)
)
meta
#>            study        region    or lower upper weight is_sum          or_text
#> 1    Chen (2016)          Asia 1.081 1.038 1.126   2065  FALSE 1.08 (1.04–1.13)
#> 2 Ibrahim (2022)          Asia 1.092 1.052 1.134   1736  FALSE 1.09 (1.05–1.13)
#> 3   Bauer (2015)        Europe 1.095 1.058 1.134    816  FALSE 1.09 (1.06–1.13)
#> 4   Evans (2018)        Europe 1.057 1.019 1.096   1041  FALSE 1.06 (1.02–1.10)
#> 5  Garcia (2020)        Europe 1.086 1.050 1.123   1479  FALSE 1.09 (1.05–1.12)
#> 6  Jensen (2023)        Europe 1.070 1.036 1.105    918  FALSE 1.07 (1.04–1.10)
#> 7 Fuentes (2019) Latin America 1.116 1.063 1.171    567  FALSE 1.12 (1.06–1.17)

Without structural arguments every row is drawn as a study:

forrest(
  meta,
  estimate  = "or",
  lower     = "lower",
  upper     = "upper",
  label     = "study",
  weight    = "weight",
  log_scale = TRUE,
  xlab      = "OR (95% CI)"
)

title: How forrest works
text:
Section expansion
When section is set, forrest() first calls build_sections(), which returns the expanded data frame that is then drawn, along with three logical vectors marking the rows it inserted.

expanded <- forrest:::build_sections(
  df             = meta,
  estimate       = "or",
  lower          = "lower",
  upper          = "upper",
  label          = "study",
  is_summary     = "is_sum",
  weight         = "weight",
  section        = "region",
  subsection     = NULL,
  section_indent = TRUE,
  section_spacer = TRUE,
  cols           = "or_text",
  section_cols   = NULL
)

expanded$df[, c("study", "region", "or", "is_sum", "or_text")]
#>               study        region    or is_sum          or_text
#> 1              Asia          <NA>    NA  FALSE                 
#> 2       Chen (2016)          Asia 1.081  FALSE 1.08 (1.04–1.13)
#> 3    Ibrahim (2022)          Asia 1.092  FALSE 1.09 (1.05–1.13)
#> 4                            <NA>    NA  FALSE                 
#> 5            Europe          <NA>    NA  FALSE                 
#> 6      Bauer (2015)        Europe 1.095  FALSE 1.09 (1.06–1.13)
#> 7      Evans (2018)        Europe 1.057  FALSE 1.06 (1.02–1.10)
#> 8     Garcia (2020)        Europe 1.086  FALSE 1.09 (1.05–1.12)
#> 9     Jensen (2023)        Europe 1.070  FALSE 1.07 (1.04–1.10)
#> 10                           <NA>    NA  FALSE                 
#> 11    Latin America          <NA>    NA  FALSE                 
#> 12   Fuentes (2019) Latin America 1.116  FALSE 1.12 (1.06–1.17)
#> 13                           <NA>    NA  FALSE


data.frame(
  study             = expanded$df$study,
  is_section_header = expanded$is_section_header,
  is_subsection_hdr = expanded$is_subsection_header,
  is_spacer         = expanded$is_spacer
)
#>               study is_section_header is_subsection_hdr is_spacer
#> 1              Asia              TRUE             FALSE     FALSE
#> 2       Chen (2016)             FALSE             FALSE     FALSE
#> 3    Ibrahim (2022)             FALSE             FALSE     FALSE
#> 4                               FALSE             FALSE      TRUE
#> 5            Europe              TRUE             FALSE     FALSE
#> 6      Bauer (2015)             FALSE             FALSE     FALSE
#> 7      Evans (2018)             FALSE             FALSE     FALSE
#> 8     Garcia (2020)             FALSE             FALSE     FALSE
#> 9     Jensen (2023)             FALSE             FALSE     FALSE
#> 10                              FALSE             FALSE      TRUE
#> 11    Latin America              TRUE             FALSE     FALSE
#> 12   Fuentes (2019)             FALSE             FALSE     FALSE
#> 13                              FALSE             FALSE      TRUE

Rows 1, 5 and 11 are the inserted headers for Asia, Europe and Latin America. Their label is the section value and their estimate is NA. A blank spacer row closes each section, the study labels are indented by two spaces, and the text column is empty on every inserted row.
Passing section = "region" to forrest() performs this expansion and draws the result:

forrest(
  meta,
  estimate  = "or",
  lower     = "lower",
  upper     = "upper",
  label     = "study",
  section   = "region",
  weight    = "weight",
  log_scale = TRUE,
  xlab      = "OR (95% CI)"
)








Before expanding, forrest() copies the group and shape columns, and a per-row col vector, into private columns. Expansion rewrites the label column, and group may name that same column; the copies keep colours and legends tied to the original values, and inserted rows get none.

Two levels
With subsection as well, build_sections() inserts a sub-header, indented by two spaces, wherever the subsection value changes within a section, and indents the data rows beneath it by four.

meta2 <- data.frame(
  region = c("Europe", "Europe", "Europe", "Europe", "Asia", "Asia"),
  design = c("Cohort", "Cohort", "Case-control", "Case-control",
             "Cohort", "Case-control"),
  study  = c("Bauer (2015)", "Evans (2018)",
             "Garcia (2020)", "Jensen (2023)",
             "Chen (2016)", "Ibrahim (2022)"),
  or     = c(1.095, 1.057, 1.086, 1.070, 1.081, 1.092),
  lower  = c(1.058, 1.019, 1.050, 1.036, 1.038, 1.052),
  upper  = c(1.134, 1.096, 1.123, 1.105, 1.126, 1.134)
)

exp2 <- forrest:::build_sections(
  df             = meta2,
  estimate       = "or",
  lower          = "lower",
  upper          = "upper",
  label          = "study",
  is_summary     = NULL,
  weight         = NULL,
  section        = "region",
  subsection     = "design",
  section_indent = TRUE,
  section_spacer = TRUE
)

data.frame(
  study                = exp2$df$study,
  is_section_header    = exp2$is_section_header,
  is_subsection_header = exp2$is_subsection_header,
  is_spacer            = exp2$is_spacer
)
#>                 study is_section_header is_subsection_header is_spacer
#> 1              Europe              TRUE                FALSE     FALSE
#> 2              Cohort             FALSE                 TRUE     FALSE
#> 3        Bauer (2015)             FALSE                FALSE     FALSE
#> 4        Evans (2018)             FALSE                FALSE     FALSE
#> 5        Case-control             FALSE                 TRUE     FALSE
#> 6       Garcia (2020)             FALSE                FALSE     FALSE
#> 7       Jensen (2023)             FALSE                FALSE     FALSE

#> 10             Cohort             FALSE                 TRUE     FALSE
#> 11        Chen (2016)             FALSE                FALSE     FALSE
#> 12       Case-control             FALSE                 TRUE     FALSE
#> 13     Ibrahim (2022)             FALSE                FALSE     FALSE

forrest(
  meta2,
  estimate   = "or",
  lower      = "lower",
  upper      = "upper",
  label      = "study",
  section    = "region",
  subsection = "design",
  log_scale  = TRUE,
  xlab       = "OR (95% CI)"

Values in header rows
section_cols fills chosen text columns on the header rows. forrest() translates its names, which are text-column headers, into the data columns those text columns display, and build_sections() writes into each one the first non-empty value of the source column among the section’s rows. Here the source column k_text holds the number of studies per section, and the displayed column k_row is empty on study rows.

meta$k_text <- c("k = 2", "", "k = 4", "", "", "", "k = 1")
meta$k_row  <- ""

exp_sc <- forrest:::build_sections(
  df             = meta,
  estimate       = "or",
  lower          = "lower",
  upper          = "upper",
  label          = "study",
  is_summary     = "is_sum",
  weight         = "weight",
  section        = "region",
  section_cols   = c(k_row = "k_text"),
  cols           = c("or_text", "k_row"),
  section_spacer = FALSE,
  section_indent = FALSE
)

exp_sc$df[, c("study", "or_text", "k_row")]
#>             study          or_text k_row
#> 1            Asia                  k = 2
#> 2     Chen (2016) 1.08 (1.04–1.13)      
#> 3  Ibrahim (2022) 1.09 (1.05–1.13)      
#> 4          Europe                  k = 4
#> 5    Bauer (2015) 1.09 (1.06–1.13)      
#> 6    Evans (2018) 1.06 (1.02–1.10)      
#> 7   Garcia (2020) 1.09 (1.05–1.12)      
#> 8   Jensen (2023) 1.07 (1.04–1.10)      
#> 9   Latin America                  k = 1
#> 10 Fuentes (2019) 1.12 (1.06–1.17)

The header rows carry the count in k_row and nothing in or_text, which section_cols does not name; study rows keep their own values.

forrest(
  meta,
  estimate     = "or",
  lower        = "lower",
  upper        = "upper",
  label        = "study",
  section      = "region",
  section_cols = c("k" = "k_text"),
  weight       = "weight",
  log_scale    = TRUE,
  header       = "Study",
  cols         = c("OR (95% CI)" = "or_text", "k" = "k_row"),
  widths       = c(3.5, 3.5, 2.2, 1.0),
  xlab         = "OR (95% CI)"
)

title: How forrest works
text:
Row types
After expansion every row is one of four types, and the type decides what is drawn. Structural rows are the inserted headers and spacers; header labels are bold. Reference rows are rows of the data whose estimate is NA; they show a plain label and no interval. Summary rows, flagged by is_summary, are drawn as diamonds. All other rows get a point and an interval. The classification for the expanded example:

df        <- expanded$df
est       <- as.numeric(df$or)
is_sum    <- as.logical(df$is_sum)
is_struct <- expanded$is_section_header |
             expanded$is_subsection_header |
             expanded$is_spacer
is_ref    <- is.na(est) & !is_sum & !is_struct
is_bold   <- (expanded$is_section_header | expanded$is_subsection_header) &
             nchar(trimws(df$study)) > 0L

data.frame(
  study     = df$study,
  is_sum    = is_sum,
  is_struct = is_struct,
  is_ref    = is_ref,
  is_bold   = is_bold,
  ci_drawn  = !is_sum & !is_struct & !is_ref
)
#>               study is_sum is_struct is_ref is_bold ci_drawn
#> 1              Asia  FALSE      TRUE  FALSE    TRUE    FALSE
#> 2       Chen (2016)  FALSE     FALSE  FALSE   FALSE     TRUE
#> 3    Ibrahim (2022)  FALSE     FALSE  FALSE   FALSE     TRUE
#> 4                    FALSE      TRUE  FALSE   FALSE    FALSE
#> 5            Europe  FALSE      TRUE  FALSE    TRUE    FALSE
#> 6      Bauer (2015)  FALSE     FALSE  FALSE   FALSE     TRUE
#> 7      Evans (2018)  FALSE     FALSE  FALSE   FALSE     TRUE
#> 8     Garcia (2020)  FALSE     FALSE  FALSE   FALSE     TRUE
#> 9     Jensen (2023)  FALSE     FALSE  FALSE   FALSE     TRUE
#> 10                   FALSE      TRUE  FALSE   FALSE    FALSE
#> 11    Latin America  FALSE      TRUE  FALSE    TRUE    FALSE
#> 12   Fuentes (2019)  FALSE     FALSE  FALSE   FALSE     TRUE
#> 13                   FALSE      TRUE  FALSE   FALSE    FALSE

This data set has no reference rows. A dose-response table has one, the reference category, and ref_label = TRUE appends “(Ref.)” to its label:

dose <- data.frame(
  quartile = c("Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4"),
  or       = c(NA,   1.21, 1.45, 1.82),
  lower    = c(NA,   1.08, 1.28, 1.60),
  upper    = c(NA,   1.36, 1.65, 2.07)
)

forrest(
  dose,
  estimate  = "or",
  lower     = "lower",
  upper     = "upper",
  label     = "quartile",
  ref_label = TRUE,
  log_scale = TRUE,
  xlab      = "OR (95% CI)"
)

title: How forrest works
text:
Summary diamonds
draw_diamond() draws each summary row as a polygon whose left and right tips are the confidence limits and whose top and bottom points sit above and below the estimate, 0.38 * cex rows from the centre. Limits beyond xlim are cut at the axis.

with_pool <- rbind(
  meta[, c("study", "region", "or", "lower", "upper", "is_sum")],
  data.frame(
    study  = "Pooled", region = "Overall",
    or     = 1.082, lower = 1.058, upper = 1.107,
    is_sum = TRUE
  )
)

forrest(
  with_pool,
  estimate   = "or",
  lower      = "lower",
  upper      = "upper",
  label      = "study",
  section    = "region",
  is_summary = "is_sum",
  log_scale  = TRUE,
  xlab       = "OR (95% CI)"
)

title: How forrest works
text:
Dodging
compute_dodge_groups() numbers the bands that rows are drawn in. A new band starts at the first row, at every change of label, and at every structural row, so headers and spacers always have a band to themselves. Without dodge, each row is its own band.

dodge_ex <- data.frame(
  label  = rep(c("Asia", "Europe"), each = 2),
  method = rep(c("Cohort", "Case-control"), 2),
  or     = c(1.08, 1.05, 1.09, 1.07),
  lower  = c(1.04, 1.01, 1.05, 1.03),
  upper  = c(1.13, 1.09, 1.14, 1.11)
)

band <- forrest:::compute_dodge_groups(dodge_ex$label,
                                       rep(FALSE, nrow(dodge_ex)))

# Bands are one unit apart, top to bottom; rows in a band are spread
# symmetrically around its centre, `dodge` units apart.
n_band <- max(band)
centre <- (n_band + 1L) - band
k      <- tabulate(band)[band]
pos    <- ave(seq_along(band), band, FUN = seq_along)
y      <- centre + (pos - (k + 1) / 2) * 0.25

data.frame(dodge_ex[, c("label", "method")], band, y)
#>    label       method band     y
#> 1   Asia       Cohort    1 1.875
#> 2   Asia Case-control    1 2.125
#> 3 Europe       Cohort    2 0.875
#> 4 Europe Case-control    2 1.125

The two Asia rows sit at 2 ± 0.125 and the two Europe rows at 1 ± 0.125:

forrest(
  dodge_ex,
  estimate  = "or",
  lower     = "lower",
  upper     = "upper",
  label     = "label",
  group     = "method",
  dodge     = TRUE,
  log_scale = TRUE,
  xlab      = "OR (95% CI)"
)

title: How forrest works
text:
Colours
group_colors() assigns colours to the distinct non-missing group values in order of appearance. By default it uses the Okabe-Ito palette from its second colour on, because the first is black and would be confused with the near-black of ungrouped rows. After eight groups the palette repeats.

forrest:::group_colors(c("Asia", "Europe", NA, "Latin America"))
#>          Asia        Europe Latin America 
#>     "#E69F00"     "#56B4E9"     "#009E73"

A col argument replaces the palette, matched by name or recycled in order:

forrest:::group_colors(c("Asia", "Europe"), c(Europe = "navy", Asia = "red"))
#>   Asia Europe 
#>  "red" "navy"

title: How forrest works
text:
Themes
resolve_theme() starts from .theme_defaults and overwrites the keys that the chosen theme or list supplies. The six keys and their defaults:

forrest:::.theme_defaults
#> $grid_col
#> [1] "#e8e8e8"
#> 
#> $grid_lty
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $grid_lwd
#> [1] 0.7
#> 
#> $ref_col
#> [1] "gray45"
#> 
#> $ref_lty
#> [1] 2
#> 
#> $stripe_col
#> [1] "#f2f2f2"

The built-in themes are lists of overrides:

forrest:::.themes
#> $default
#> list()
#> 
#> $minimal
#> $minimal$grid_col
#> [1] "#f0f0f0"
#> 
#> $minimal$grid_lwd
#> [1] 0.5
#> 
#> $minimal$ref_col
#> [1] "#777777"
#> 
#> 
#> $classic
#> $classic$grid_col
#> [1] "lightgray"
#> 
#> $classic$grid_lty
#> [1] 3
#> 
#> $classic$grid_lwd
#> [1] 0.7
#> 
#> $classic$ref_col
#> [1] "black"
#> 
#> $classic$ref_lty
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $classic$stripe_col
#> [1] "#efefef"

A list passed as theme overrides only the keys it names, and an unknown key is an error:

dat <- data.frame(
  label    = c("A", "B", "C"),
  estimate = c(0.2, -0.1, 0.4),
  lower    = c(0.0, -0.3, 0.2),
  upper    = c(0.4,  0.1, 0.6)
)

forrest(
  dat,
  estimate = "estimate",
  lower    = "lower",
  upper    = "upper",
  label    = "label",
  theme    = list(ref_col = "#e63946", ref_lty = 1L,
                  grid_col = "#eeeeee", stripe_col = "#fafafa"),
  stripe   = TRUE,
  xlab     = "Coefficient (95% CI)"
)

title: Forest plots for regression models
text: This vignette goes from fitted models to forest plots. broom::tidy() turns a model into a data frame of estimates and confidence limits, which forrest() plots directly; any other function that returns such a data frame works as well. The last sections use marginaleffects to estimate average treatment effects by g-computation and inverse probability weighting.

title: Forest plots for regression models
text:
Simulated cohort
All examples use one simulated cohort of 800 adults. Systolic blood pressure (SBP) rises with age and BMI and is lower in women, smokers and physically active people; hypertension is defined as SBP of 140 mmHg or more.

set.seed(42)
n <- 800

cohort <- data.frame(
  age      = round(runif(n, 30, 75)),
  female   = rbinom(n, 1, 0.52),
  bmi      = rnorm(n, 26, 4.5),
  smoker   = rbinom(n, 1, 0.20),
  activity = rbinom(n, 1, 0.45),   # 1 = physically active
  educ     = factor(
    sample(c("Low", "Medium", "High"), n,
           replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.25, 0.45, 0.30)),
    levels = c("Low", "Medium", "High")
  )
)

cohort$sbp <- 110 +
  0.40 * cohort$age    -
  4.50 * cohort$female +
  0.50 * cohort$bmi    -
  2.00 * cohort$smoker -
  2.50 * cohort$activity +
  rnorm(n, sd = 8)

cohort$htn <- as.integer(cohort$sbp >= 140)

title: Forest plots for regression models
text:
Several predictors from one model
broom::tidy(conf.int = TRUE) returns the columns estimate, conf.low and conf.high, which map onto the estimate, lower and upper arguments. Drop the intercept and replace the term names with readable labels.

fit_lm <- lm(sbp ~ age + female + bmi + smoker + activity, data = cohort)

coefs <- broom::tidy(fit_lm, conf.int = TRUE)
coefs <- coefs[coefs$term != "(Intercept)", ]
coefs$term <- c(
  "Age (per 1 year)",
  "Female sex",
  "BMI (per 1 kg/m²)",
  "Current smoker",
  "Physically active"
)

coefs$coef_ci <- sprintf(
  "%.2f (%.2f, %.2f)",
  coefs$estimate, coefs$conf.low, coefs$conf.high
)

forrest(
  coefs,
  estimate = "estimate",
  lower    = "conf.low",
  upper    = "conf.high",
  label    = "term",
  header   = "Predictor",
  cols     = c("Coef (95% CI)" = "coef_ci"),
  widths   = c(3, 4, 2.5),
  xlab     = "Difference in SBP, mmHg (95% CI)",
  stripe   = TRUE
)








For a logistic model, exponentiate = TRUE in broom::tidy() returns odds ratios, and log_scale = TRUE in forrest() draws them on a log axis with the reference line at 1.

fit_glm <- glm(htn ~ age + female + bmi + smoker + activity,
               data = cohort, family = binomial)

or_coefs <- broom::tidy(fit_glm, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE)
or_coefs <- or_coefs[or_coefs$term != "(Intercept)", ]
or_coefs$term <- c(
  "Age (per 1 year)",
  "Female sex",
  "BMI (per 1 kg/m²)",
  "Current smoker",
  "Physically active"
)

or_coefs$or_text <- sprintf(
  "%.2f (%.2f, %.2f)",
  or_coefs$estimate, or_coefs$conf.low, or_coefs$conf.high
)

forrest(
  or_coefs,
  estimate   = "estimate",
  lower      = "conf.low",
  upper      = "conf.high",
  label      = "term",
  log_scale  = TRUE,
  header     = "Predictor",
  cols       = c("OR (95% CI)" = "or_text"),
  widths     = c(3, 4, 2),
  xlab       = "Odds ratio for hypertension (95% CI)"
)

title: Forest plots for regression models
text:
One exposure across adjustment sets
Papers often show how an association changes as covariates are added. Fit one model per adjustment set, keep the exposure’s row from each, and stack the rows.

m1 <- glm(htn ~ activity,
          data = cohort, family = binomial)
m2 <- glm(htn ~ activity + age + female,
          data = cohort, family = binomial)
m3 <- glm(htn ~ activity + age + female + bmi + smoker,
          data = cohort, family = binomial)

extract_activity <- function(mod, label) {
  row       <- broom::tidy(mod, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE)
  row       <- row[row$term == "activity", ]
  row$model <- label
  row
}

adj_dat <- rbind(
  extract_activity(m1, "Model 1: unadjusted"),
  extract_activity(m2, "Model 2: + age, sex"),
  extract_activity(m3, "Model 3: + BMI, smoking")
)

adj_dat$or_text <- sprintf(
  "%.2f (%.2f, %.2f)",
  adj_dat$estimate, adj_dat$conf.low, adj_dat$conf.high
)

forrest(
  adj_dat,
  estimate   = "estimate",
  lower      = "conf.low",
  upper      = "conf.high",
  label      = "model",
  log_scale  = TRUE,
  header     = "Adjustment set",
  cols       = c("OR (95% CI)" = "or_text"),
  widths     = c(4, 3.5, 2),
  xlab       = "OR of hypertension, active vs inactive (95% CI)"
)

title: Forest plots for regression models
text:
One exposure across several outcomes
To compare one exposure across outcomes, fit one model per outcome and stack the exposure rows. Differences from linear models and odds ratios from logistic models do not share a scale or a null value, so they go in separate plots: one with a linear axis and reference line at 0, one with a log axis and reference line at 1.

outcomes <- data.frame(
  var   = c("sbp", "bmi", "htn", "smoker"),
  label = c("Systolic BP (mmHg)", "BMI (kg/m²)",
            "Hypertension", "Current smoker"),
  type  = c("continuous", "continuous", "binary", "binary")
)

multi_out <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(outcomes)), function(i) {
  o   <- outcomes[i, ]
  fml <- as.formula(paste(o$var, "~ activity + age + female"))
  r <- if (o$type == "continuous") {
    broom::tidy(lm(fml, data = cohort), conf.int = TRUE)
  } else {
    broom::tidy(glm(fml, data = cohort, family = binomial),
                conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE)
  }
  r         <- r[r$term == "activity", ]
  r$outcome <- o$label
  r$type    <- o$type
  r
}))

multi_out$est_text <- sprintf(
  "%.2f (%.2f, %.2f)",
  multi_out$estimate, multi_out$conf.low, multi_out$conf.high
)

forrest(
  multi_out[multi_out$type == "continuous", ],
  estimate   = "estimate",
  lower      = "conf.low",
  upper      = "conf.high",
  label      = "outcome",
  header     = "Outcome",
  cols       = c("Difference (95% CI)" = "est_text"),
  widths     = c(3.5, 3.5, 2.5),
  xlab       = "Difference, active vs inactive (95% CI)"
)








forrest(
  multi_out[multi_out$type == "binary", ],
  estimate   = "estimate",
  lower      = "conf.low",
  upper      = "conf.high",
  label      = "outcome",
  log_scale  = TRUE,
  header     = "Outcome",
  cols       = c("OR (95% CI)" = "est_text"),
  widths     = c(3.5, 3.5, 2.5),
  xlab       = "Odds ratio, active vs inactive (95% CI)"
)

title: Forest plots for regression models
text:
Exposure categories
A categorical exposure, here age quartiles, has a reference category with no estimate of its own. A row whose estimate is NA is drawn as a label without an interval, which keeps the reference category visible in its place; ref_label = TRUE appends “(Ref.)” to its label. The quartile labels are built from the cut points, so they stay correct if the data change.

breaks  <- quantile(cohort$age, 0:4 / 4)
q_names <- sprintf("Q%d (%g–%g y)", 1:4, breaks[1:4], breaks[2:5])
cohort$age_q <- cut(cohort$age, breaks = breaks,
                    include.lowest = TRUE, labels = q_names)

fit_q   <- glm(htn ~ age_q + female + bmi + smoker + activity,
               data = cohort, family = binomial)
q_coefs <- broom::tidy(fit_q, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE)
q_coefs <- q_coefs[startsWith(q_coefs$term, "age_q"), ]

q_plot <- data.frame(
  label     = q_names,
  estimate  = c(NA, q_coefs$estimate),
  conf.low  = c(NA, q_coefs$conf.low),
  conf.high = c(NA, q_coefs$conf.high)
)
q_plot$or_ci <- ifelse(
  is.na(q_plot$estimate),
  "1.00",
  sprintf("%.2f (%.2f, %.2f)",
          q_plot$estimate, q_plot$conf.low, q_plot$conf.high)
)

forrest(
  q_plot,
  estimate   = "estimate",
  lower      = "conf.low",
  upper      = "conf.high",
  label      = "label",
  ref_label  = TRUE,
  log_scale  = TRUE,
  header     = "Age quartile",
  cols       = c("OR (95% CI)" = "or_ci"),
  widths     = c(3, 4, 2),
  xlab       = "OR for hypertension (95% CI)"
)

title: Forest plots for regression models
text:
Average treatment effects by g-computation
Parametric g-computation estimates the average treatment effect (ATE) by predicting every person’s outcome twice, once as if active and once as if inactive, and averaging the differences. marginaleffects::avg_comparisons() does this in one call. Here the outcome model lets the effect of activity vary with each covariate, and the ATE is estimated overall and within strata of sex and education by averaging over the people in each stratum.

library(marginaleffects)

fit_sbp <- lm(
  sbp ~ activity * (age + female + bmi + smoker + educ),
  data = cohort
)

strata <- list(
  list(stratum = "Overall",   label = "Overall",
       rows = rep(TRUE, n),          is_sum = TRUE),
  list(stratum = "Sex",       label = "Female",
       rows = cohort$female == 1,    is_sum = FALSE),
  list(stratum = "Sex",       label = "Male",
       rows = cohort$female == 0,    is_sum = FALSE),
  list(stratum = "Education", label = "Low",
       rows = cohort$educ == "Low",    is_sum = FALSE),
  list(stratum = "Education", label = "Medium",
       rows = cohort$educ == "Medium", is_sum = FALSE),
  list(stratum = "Education", label = "High",
       rows = cohort$educ == "High",   is_sum = FALSE)
)

gcomp_dat <- do.call(rbind, lapply(strata, function(s) {
  me <- avg_comparisons(fit_sbp, variables = "activity",
                        newdata = cohort[s$rows, ])
  data.frame(
    stratum  = s$stratum,
    label    = s$label,
    estimate = me$estimate,
    lower    = me$conf.low,
    upper    = me$conf.high,
    is_sum   = s$is_sum
  )
}))

gcomp_dat$est_text <- sprintf(
  "%.2f (%.2f, %.2f)",
  gcomp_dat$estimate, gcomp_dat$lower, gcomp_dat$upper
)

forrest(
  gcomp_dat,
  estimate   = "estimate",
  lower      = "lower",
  upper      = "upper",
  label      = "label",
  section    = "stratum",
  is_summary = "is_sum",
  cols       = c("ATE (95% CI)" = "est_text"),
  widths     = c(3.5, 4, 3),
  header     = "Stratum",
  xlab       = "ATE of physical activity on SBP, mmHg (95% CI)"
)

title: Forest plots for regression models
section: Comparing g-computation with inverse probability weighting
text:
Comparing g-computation with inverse probability weighting
Inverse probability weighting (IPW) models who is active rather than how SBP depends on the covariates. Each person is weighted by the inverse of the probability of the activity level they were observed to have, which balances the measured confounders between active and inactive people. Following the marginaleffects IPW chapter, the outcome model is refitted with these weights, and avg_comparisons() averages the contrasts with the same weights.
Plotting both estimators in one figure shows whether they agree. Each stratum has two rows, one per method, so dodge = TRUE draws them as a pair of intervals within one band and cols_by_group = TRUE gives each method its own text column.

ps_mod    <- glm(activity ~ age + female + bmi + smoker + educ,
                 data = cohort, family = binomial)
cohort$ps <- predict(ps_mod, type = "response")
cohort$ipw <- ifelse(cohort$activity == 1, 1 / cohort$ps, 1 / (1 - cohort$ps))

# Truncate the weights at their 1st and 99th percentiles
cohort$ipw_t <- pmin(pmax(cohort$ipw, quantile(cohort$ipw, 0.01)),
                     quantile(cohort$ipw, 0.99))

fit_sbp_ipw <- lm(
  sbp ~ activity * (age + female + bmi + smoker + educ),
  data = cohort, weights = ipw_t
)

compare_dat <- do.call(rbind, lapply(strata, function(s) {
  nd  <- cohort[s$rows, ]
  gc  <- avg_comparisons(fit_sbp, variables = "activity", newdata = nd)
  ipw <- avg_comparisons(fit_sbp_ipw, variables = "activity",
                         wts = "ipw_t", newdata = nd)
  data.frame(
    label    = s$label,
    method   = c("G-computation", "IPW"),
    estimate = c(gc$estimate,  ipw$estimate),
    lower    = c(gc$conf.low,  ipw$conf.low),
    upper    = c(gc$conf.high, ipw$conf.high),
    is_sum   = s$is_sum
  )
}))

est_text <- sprintf("%.2f (%.2f, %.2f)", compare_dat$estimate,
                    compare_dat$lower, compare_dat$upper)
compare_dat$text_gc  <- ifelse(compare_dat$method == "G-computation",
                               est_text, "")
compare_dat$text_ipw <- ifelse(compare_dat$method == "IPW", est_text, "")

forrest(
  compare_dat,
  estimate      = "estimate",
  lower         = "lower",
  upper         = "upper",
  label         = "label",
  group         = "method",
  is_summary    = "is_sum",
  dodge         = TRUE,
  cols_by_group = TRUE,
  cols          = c("G-computation (95% CI)" = "text_gc",
                    "IPW (95% CI)"           = "text_ipw"),
  widths        = c(3, 3.5, 2.5, 2.5),
  header        = "Stratum",
  xlab          = "ATE of physical activity on SBP, mmHg (95% CI)"
)








The IPW intervals treat the weights as known. They ignore the uncertainty from estimating the propensity score; a bootstrap over both steps would account for it.

title: Forest plots for regression models
text:
Estimates over time
Analyses that produce one estimate per time point, such as distributed lag models, life-course analyses and repeated measures, give a data frame in which time is one more column. section, group and dodge arrange them like any other grouping.

Distributed lag models
A distributed lag model estimates the association at each lag between exposure and outcome. Here section = "exposure" groups the lags under each exposure, and the cumulative estimate over all lags closes each section as a diamond.

set.seed(2025)

make_lags <- function(pattern) {
  se  <- runif(length(pattern), 0.03, 0.06)
  est <- pattern + rnorm(length(pattern), sd = 0.02)
  data.frame(
    estimate = est,
    lower    = est - 1.96 * se,
    upper    = est + 1.96 * se
  )
}

lag_labels <- paste("Lag", 0:6, "(weeks)")

dlm_dat <- rbind(
  data.frame(exposure = "PM2.5", lag = lag_labels, is_sum = FALSE,
             make_lags(c(0.04, 0.11, 0.10, 0.06, 0.03, 0.01, 0.00))),
  data.frame(exposure = "PM2.5", lag = "Cumulative", is_sum = TRUE,
             estimate = 0.35, lower = 0.18, upper = 0.52),
  data.frame(exposure = "Road noise", lag = lag_labels, is_sum = FALSE,
             make_lags(c(0.09, 0.05, 0.02, 0.01, 0.00, -0.01, 0.00))),
  data.frame(exposure = "Road noise", lag = "Cumulative", is_sum = TRUE,
             estimate = 0.16, lower = 0.04, upper = 0.28),
  data.frame(exposure = "Green space", lag = lag_labels, is_sum = FALSE,
             make_lags(c(-0.02, -0.04, -0.07, -0.09, -0.10, -0.09, -0.08))),
  data.frame(exposure = "Green space", lag = "Cumulative", is_sum = TRUE,
             estimate = -0.49, lower = -0.68, upper = -0.30)
)

dlm_dat$est_text <- sprintf("%.2f (%.2f, %.2f)",
                            dlm_dat$estimate, dlm_dat$lower, dlm_dat$upper)

forrest(
  dlm_dat,
  estimate   = "estimate",
  lower      = "lower",
  upper      = "upper",
  label      = "lag",
  section    = "exposure",
  is_summary = "is_sum",
  header     = "Lag",
  cols       = c("Coef (95% CI)" = "est_text"),
  widths     = c(3.5, 4, 2.8),
  xlab       = "Difference in SBP per IQR increase, mmHg (95% CI)"
)










Life-course analysis by stage
A life-course analysis estimates the same associations at several developmental stages. With section = "life_stage" each stage is a section listing the exposures, and group = "exposure" gives each exposure the same colour in every stage.

set.seed(99)

stage_row <- function(exposure, life_stage, est, se) {
  est <- est + rnorm(1, sd = 0.01)
  data.frame(
    life_stage = life_stage,
    exposure   = exposure,
    estimate   = est,
    lower      = est - 1.96 * se,
    upper      = est + 1.96 * se
  )
}

lc_dat <- rbind(
  stage_row("Noise exposure",      "Prenatal",         0.08, 0.03),
  stage_row("Green space access",  "Prenatal",        -0.05, 0.04),
  stage_row("Traffic-related air", "Prenatal",         0.06, 0.03),
  stage_row("Noise exposure",      "Early childhood",  0.12, 0.04),
  stage_row("Green space access",  "Early childhood", -0.09, 0.05),
  stage_row("Traffic-related air", "Early childhood",  0.10, 0.04),
  stage_row("Noise exposure",      "Mid-childhood",    0.15, 0.05),
  stage_row("Green space access",  "Mid-childhood",   -0.13, 0.05),
  stage_row("Traffic-related air", "Mid-childhood",    0.14, 0.05),
  stage_row("Noise exposure",      "Adolescence",      0.09, 0.04),
  stage_row("Green space access",  "Adolescence",     -0.07, 0.05),
  stage_row("Traffic-related air", "Adolescence",      0.08, 0.04)
)

forrest(
  lc_dat,
  estimate = "estimate",
  lower    = "lower",
  upper    = "upper",
  label    = "exposure",
  section  = "life_stage",
  group    = "exposure",
  legend_pos = NULL,
  header   = "Exposure",
  xlab     = "Difference in SBP per IQR increase, mmHg (95% CI)"
)








The colour legend is turned off with legend_pos = NULL because the labels already name the exposures.


Life-course analysis by exposure
To compare stages within each exposure instead, sort the same data by exposure, label the rows by exposure, colour them by stage, and dodge the stages within each exposure’s band.

stages <- c("Prenatal", "Early childhood", "Mid-childhood", "Adolescence")
lc_by_exposure <- lc_dat[order(lc_dat$exposure,
                               match(lc_dat$life_stage, stages)), ]

forrest(
  lc_by_exposure,
  estimate = "estimate",
  lower    = "lower",
  upper    = "upper",
  label    = "exposure",
  group    = "life_stage",
  dodge    = TRUE,
  header   = "Exposure",
  xlab     = "Difference in SBP per IQR increase, mmHg (95% CI)"
)
